primer.intro: A string is an array of characters, and almost every beginner string problem is one scan from left to right with a little state carried along: a counter, the previous character, a small frequency table. The difficulty is rarely the algorithm - it is deciding what the state must remember. Nesting depth is a counter that rises on an opening bracket and falls on a closing one. Roman numerals need one glance at the next symbol. Parsing a number needs a sign, an accumulator and a stopping rule. This topic trains that reflex: before writing any loop, say out loud what you must know at position i to act, then carry exactly that and nothing more.
whenToUse: The answer is a property of one pass: a depth, a count, a running best.
A decision at position i needs only a constant-size peek at a neighbour.
The task is parsing: skip, sign, digits, stopping rule, clamp.
Palindromes of unknown length are involved; centres are easier than ends.
Substring statistics are summed; fix the start, extend the end with a frequency table.
primer.mentalModel: Think of the scan as a tiny machine walking the string once. At each character it may consult its state, update that state, and sometimes emit something - a character to the output, a new best-so-far. Counters handle anything bracket-shaped: depth is the counter itself, and the outermost brackets of a block are exactly the characters whose step leaves or returns to zero. Peeking handles subtractive notation: a roman symbol smaller than its successor is a subtraction. When one scan is too weak because the answer spans two directions, pick centres instead of ends - a palindrome grows symmetrically outward from each of its 2n minus 1 centres, so expanding from every centre visits each candidate once.
mistakes: Peeking at position i plus 1 while standing on the last character - guard the index before comparing.
Growing a result by string concatenation inside the loop, a quadratic bill in some languages; collect pieces and join once.
Treating the character 7 as the number 7; subtract the code of the zero digit or convert explicitly.

example.title: Nesting depth in one scan
example.explain: The counter is the whole state. An opening bracket pushes the depth up and the best-so-far updates immediately; a closing bracket pulls it down. Letters and digits fall through untouched, which is why the same loop handles expressions that mix brackets with other text. One pass, constant extra space - and the identical skeleton solves the outermost-parentheses task by copying a bracket only when its step keeps the counter inside the block.

primer.practice: Open Practice and start with Remove Outermost Parentheses - the depth counter there reappears in four of the six problems.

sections.title: One scan, one counter
sections.text: Before coding, name the state. For depth questions it is a single integer; for frequency questions a 26-slot table; for parsing, a sign and an accumulator. Then write the transition: what happens to that state at an opener, a digit, a letter? The outermost-parentheses trick is worth memorising as a specimen: increment on an opener, decrement on a closer, and a bracket belongs to the outer shell exactly when the counter crosses zero on that step. Everything interior is copied; the shell is skipped. No stack is needed, because with one bracket type the counter is a stack whose entries are all identical.

check.prompt: Scanning (()(())) with a depth counter that rises on ( and falls on ), what is the maximum depth reached?

options.explain: The fifth character is a third unmatched opener: depths run 1 2 1 2 3 2 1 0.
Two is a peak the counter visits twice, but the inner (( climbs past it.
Four would need four openers stacked at one moment; at most three are open.
Zero is the final value - it confirms balance, it does not measure depth.

reveal.solution: Walk it: ( depth 1, ( depth 2, ) depth 1, ( depth 2, ( depth 3, ) depth 2, ) depth 1, ) depth 0. The counter peaks at 3 on the fifth character, where three brackets are open at once. The final 0 says every opener found its closer - balance - while the recorded peak is the nesting depth the question wants.

sections.title: Peek at the neighbour
sections.text: Some encodings place meaning in a pair of adjacent characters. Roman numerals subtract whenever a smaller value stands before a larger one, so the scan compares each symbol with its successor: smaller means subtract it, otherwise add it, and the last symbol is always added. Parsing an integer is the same reflex pointed at a prefix: skip blanks, read one optional sign, then consume digits while they last, multiplying the accumulator by ten before each new digit - and test the 32-bit clamp before that multiplication, because afterwards the damage is already done. Both scans stop the moment the pattern breaks, and stopping quietly is part of the contract.

quiz.prompt: Remove the outermost parentheses of every block in a string of ( and ). Which tool fits best?

options.text: A depth counter; copy a bracket only when its step stays inside the block
options.explain: Shell brackets are exactly the steps that leave or return to depth zero.

options.text: A stack holding every open bracket's index
options.explain: Works, but with one bracket type the count carries all the information.
Nesting of unbounded depth is beyond a single pattern pass.
Correct yet heavy; the one-pass counter does it with no call stack.

quiz.prompt: A roman numeral mixes shapes like IV and VI. What single rule decodes the whole string?

options.text: Compare each symbol with the next: smaller before larger subtracts, otherwise add
options.explain: IV is 5 minus 1 because I stands before the larger V; the last symbol always adds.
IX would read as 11; the subtractive pairs need the comparison.

options.text: Scan right to left and always subtract
options.explain: Direction alone fixes nothing - the add-or-subtract choice still needs a rule.

options.text: Look the whole numeral up in a table
options.explain: Thousands of numerals exist; the pairwise rule covers them all in one line.

quiz.prompt: Longest palindromic substring, length up to 1000. Which plan is the standard beginner answer?

options.text: Expand around each of the 2n-1 centres and keep the widest match
options.explain: Every palindrome has a centre; expanding from all of them covers every candidate.

options.text: Test every substring for being a palindrome
options.explain: n squared substrings times a linear check is cubic - hopeless at 1000.

options.text: Take the longest common substring with the reversed string
options.explain: A classic trap: a reversed copy elsewhere can match without being a palindrome.
Order is the whole question; sorting destroys it.

quiz.prompt: Sum the beauty of all substrings, where beauty is top frequency minus bottom frequency. Plan?

options.text: Fix each start, extend the end, update a 26-slot table, add the beauty per step
options.explain: Each extension changes one count; the table makes every substring cheap.

options.text: Materialise every substring and count its letters from scratch
options.explain: Cubic time and heavy allocation; the table version reuses all prior work.

options.text: Keep one global frequency table for the whole string
options.explain: Beauty is a per-substring quantity; one global table blurs them together.
No monotone rule says when to shrink - every substring must be visited here.

quiz.prompt: A depth scan runs over (a(b)((c))). What maximum does it record?

options.explain: At c three brackets are open: the outer one plus the double opener.
Two is reached at b, but the (( after it climbs one higher.
Count only brackets open at once - letters never raise the counter.
Zero is where the counter ends, by balance; the peak is what is recorded.
XL is 40 because X precedes the larger L; IX is 9 for the same reason.
That adds 10, 50, 1, 10 blindly - both subtractive pairs were missed.
XL decoded, IX missed: 40 plus 10 plus 9 double-counts the I.
That drops the final X entirely instead of folding it into IX.

quiz.prompt: Run the standard atoi scan on the line "  -042abc". What does it return?

options.explain: Blanks skipped, one sign taken, the leading zero is harmless, the scan stops at a.
The minus sign was consumed and must flip the result.
Trailing letters do nothing to the prefix already parsed - only a missing digit gives 0.
Stopping quietly at the first letter is the contract; throwing is needless.

quiz.prompt: Expand-around-centre on a string of length n: time and extra space?

options.explain: 2n-1 centres, each expanding up to n steps; only two indices are stored.
A linear-time answer exists but needs Manacher's machinery, a later tool.
Nothing is tabulated; the expansion keeps two moving indices only.
Cubic is the test-every-substring plan this one replaces.

quiz.prompt: The beauty sum with a per-start frequency table: how much work in total?

options.explain: n starts, up to n extensions each, and a 26-slot sweep after every extension.
There are about n squared over 2 substrings to account for - linear is impossible.
Substrings are contiguous, so n squared of them exist, no more.

options.text: n squared with no constant at all
options.explain: The honest cost keeps the 26-sweep; dropping it hides real work.

quiz.prompt: This decoder returns 11 for IX. What is the bug?

options.text: Subtractive pairs are missed: a symbol smaller than its successor must subtract
options.explain: Compare v of the current symbol with v of the next; smaller-first means minus.
The seven values are the standard ones.

options.text: The loop must run right to left
options.explain: Left to right is fine - the missing piece is the neighbour comparison.
IX is the canonical way to write 9.

quiz.prompt: On 32-bit integers this parser clamps too late. Why?

options.text: r can overflow inside the loop; the guard must run before each multiply-and-add
options.explain: Once fixed-width r wraps, the final comparison inspects garbage.

options.text: The clamp constant is off by one
options.explain: 2147483647 is the correct positive limit.

options.text: The loop must consume digits right to left
options.explain: Place value is already handled by the multiply by ten.

options.text: The clamp belongs to the caller
options.explain: Where it lives is style; running it after the wrap is the real fault.

quiz.prompt: Which input most deserves a dedicated test for a longest-palindrome routine?

options.explain: The answer must be 1, and every centre loop must survive width-zero expansion.
Random inputs exercise nothing in particular.
The character set is irrelevant to palindromes.
Sortedness has no palindromic meaning.
